explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose
   - This is an open-source, multi-language compression library implementing the Brotli algorithm (RFC 7932).  
   - It provides a high-performance core in C (encode/decode), a command-line tool, fuzz & research harnesses, and language bindings (C#, Java, Go, JS, Python).

2. Analyze the file structure
   - Top-level:
     • BUILD.bazel, CMakeLists.txt, scripts/ → build & install (Bazel, CMake, scripts for pkgconfig)  
     • c/ → core C implementation, subdivided into common/, enc/, dec/  
     • c/include/brotli/ → public C API headers  
     • c/tools/ → brotli CLI tool based on the core  
     • c/fuzz/ → fuzzing harness targeting the C core  
     • research/ → experimental tools, dumps, generators  
     • {csharp, java, go, js, python}/ → language wrappers & pure-language ports  
     • tests/ → compatibility & round-trip tests for the C core and testdata  
   - Each language folder contains its own BUILD/MODULE files (Bazel), tests, and binding code.

3. Examine the README
   - Confirms Brotli’s algorithmic building blocks (LZ77 variant, Huffman, context modeling).  
   - Lists build instructions (vcpkg, Bazel, CMake, pip).  
   - Points to related projects and benchmarks—no higher-level architecture diagram is provided.

4. How to create the system design diagram
   a. Main components
      • Core Compression Engine (C library)  
         – dec/ + enc/ modules, common utilities, public API (include/brotli)  
      • Build & CI  
         – Bazel, CMake, scripts, GitHub Actions workflows, OSS-Fuzz  
      • CLI Tool  
         – c/tools/brotli  
      • Fuzzing Harness  
         – c/fuzz  
      • Research Tools  
         – research/  
      • Language Bindings & Ports  
         – C#: pure C# port (csharp/)  
         – Java: pure Java implementation (java/org/brotli/dec & enc/)  
         – Java JNI wrapper (java/org/brotli/wrapper/* + .cc bridge)  
         – Go: pure Go port (go/brotli) + cgo wrapper (go/cbrotli)  
         – JavaScript/TypeScript port (js/)  
         – Python C extension + pure Python entrypoint (python/)  
      • Tests  
         – Unit/integration tests under each language folder and tests/ for C core  

   b. Relationships / interactions
      • All language bindings either link directly to the C core (via JNI, cgo, Python C-API) or reimplement it in the target language.  
      • The CLI tool links against the C core and exposes a user-facing binary.  
      • Fuzz harness and tests drive the C core APIs.  
      • Research tools depend on the core C library to explore algorithm internals and generate artifacts.  
      • Build system orchestrates compilation of core, wrappers, tests, tools, fuzzers across all platforms.

   c. Architectural patterns / design principles
      • Layered architecture: core engine at center, adapter/bridge layers for each language.  
      • Adapter (wrapper) pattern for JNI, cgo, Python C-API, PInvoke-style.  
      • Modular separation of encode vs. decode vs. shared utilities.  
      • Reusable public API (include/brotli) for all clients.  

   d. Key technologies / frameworks / libraries
      • Languages: C, C++, Java, Kotlin, C#, Go, TypeScript/JavaScript, Python  
      • Build: Bazel, CMake, setuptools/python packaging, npm (for js), Maven/Gradle (Java)  
      • Interop: JNI, cgo, Python C-API, PInvoke  
      • CI/Fuzz: GitHub Actions, OSS-Fuzz  

5. Guidelines for tailoring the diagram (Open-source library focus)
   - Center on the core engine and show each binding as an extension or alternative implementation.  
   - Emphasize the public C API as the single integration point.  
   - Illustrate how tests, fuzzers, and tools reuse the core.  
   - Show build & CI orchestrating all components.

6. Diagram elements to include
   - Clear, concise labels for each component (e.g., “Brotli C Core,” “Java Wrapper (JNI),” “Pure Go Port”).  
   - Directional arrows to show:
     – API calls from wrappers → core  
     – Test harnesses / CLI → core  
     – Build system → all modules  
   - Color-coding or shapes to differentiate:
     – Core (e.g., shaded central circle)  
     – Language bindings (distinct colors per language)  
     – Tools & tests (different shape, e.g., rectangles)  
     – Build/CI (icon or banner around diagram)

7. Emphasis
   - Be exhaustive: list every major module (enc, dec, common, wrappers, tools).  
   - Capture integration points: public API headers, JNI/cgo/Python bridges.  
   - Show data flow (compression & decompression) through the core.  
   - Ensure the diagram remains readable by grouping related components (e.g., all Java bits in one cluster).
</explanation>
